terms.meaning: Cornwallis's 1793 system in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha: zamindars collected a fixed land tax as government agents.
Farmers paid land tax straight to the government, with no middlemen.
Land tax fixed for a whole mahal (village or estate), collected by the local zamindar.
Dadabhai Navroji's idea that India grew poor because huge wealth flowed to England.
Rule shared between two authorities. The 1935 Act brought it in at the Centre.

items.name: Warren Hastings' bidding system
items.formula: Tax collection went to the highest bidder.
items.example: Zamindars bid high but couldn't collect, so income varied.

items.name: Effect of the Permanent System on farmers
items.formula: Zamindars overtaxed them, didn't improve farming, and demanded tax even when crops failed.
items.example: Output fell and bonded labour grew.

items.name: Ryotwari details
items.formula: Brought in by Sir Thomas Munroe in Madras province in 1801, in South and West India.
items.example: Tax was half the produce, due even after floods or drought.

items.name: Mahalwari details
items.formula: Began in 1833 in Uttar Pradesh, parts of Madhya Pradesh and Punjab.

items.name: Overall effect of British land policy
items.formula: Land became something to buy and sell; cash crops replaced food crops.
items.example: Cotton, jute and tobacco paid the British, but caused food shortage.

items.name: Charter Act of 1813
items.formula: Set aside one lakh rupees for Indians' education.

items.name: Medium of instruction
items.formula: In 1835 William Bentick chose English and western science, based on Macaulay's note.
items.example: Macaulay looked down on Indian knowledge.

items.name: Europeans who praised Indian culture
items.formula: William Jones founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784); Charles Wilkins translated the Bhagavadgita (1785).
items.example: Max Muller translated the Rig Veda.

items.name: Wood's education policy
items.formula: The 1854 policy, from Charles Wood's report; universities at Bombay, Calcutta and Madras in 1857.
items.example: English became the official language in 1844.

items.name: Effects of western education
items.formula: Indians of different languages could talk in English, which helped nationalism.
items.example: Traditional education declined; new literary movements began.

items.name: British trade policy
items.formula: India was to export raw materials and import British machine goods.
items.example: Open trade pushed Indian cottage industries towards ruin; Adam Smith called the British "plunderers".

items.name: Regulating Act and Pitt's India Act
items.formula: 1773: the first milestone, a constitution for the Company. 1784: William Pitt made the Company part of the government.
items.example: Warren Hastings put the 1773 Act into effect.

items.name: Morley-Minto Reforms (1909)
items.formula: Enlarged the central and provincial legislatures and let some Indians in.
items.example: They gave no real responsibility to people's representatives.

items.name: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919)
items.formula: Followed Montagu's 1917 promise of more Indian representation and self-government.
items.example: A High Commissioner for India was appointed in London.

items.name: Government of India Act 1935
items.formula: A federation of states and provinces; diarchy at the Centre; responsible governments in provinces.

mistakes.text: Permanent: Cornwallis, zamindars. Ryotwari: Munroe, farmers pay directly. Mahalwari: tax per village.
Paying tax directly (Ryotwari) did not make it lighter: the tax was still very high.
The policy was 1854, but the three universities opened in 1857.
